head.ce:title: The amidoxime-functionalized magnetic dendritic fibrous nano-silica with a core–shell structure for the efficient capture of U(VI)

ce:list-item.ce:para: A novel amidoxime-functionalized magnetic nanoparticle (Fe3O4@DFNS-AO) with core–shell and fibrous structure was fabricated.
The fibrous and open pores of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO facilitate the transfer and diffusion of U(VI) ions.
Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exhibited fast adsorption kinetics and good selectivity toward U(VI).

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The U(VI) extraction from nuclear wastewater through adsorption techniques is vital for reclaiming uranium resources and mitigating environmental pollution. Herein, amidoxime-functionalized dendritic fibrous nano-silica with magnetic reponsiveness and core–shell structure (Fe3O4@DFNS-AO) was synthesized. The rapid absorption of U(VI) by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO achieved equilibrium within 40 min. Fe3O4@DFNS-AO showed great adsorption efficiency, as well as good reusability and selectivity, with a capacity of 175.4 mg/g at optimal pH 6.0. Furthermore, the mechanism was disclosed based upon the study of adsorption behavior and XPS analysis. The study of kinetic and isotherm indicated chemisorption dominated the adsorption and U(VI) could be adsorbed onto Fe3O4@DFNS-AO by monolayer. The amidoxime groups in Fe3O4@DFNS-AO acted as electron donors and formed coordination bonds with uranyl ions, leading to the efficient capture of U(VI). Overall, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO shows great promise in extracting uranium from wastewater.

ce:section.ce:para: Nuclear energy, known for its low carbon emissions and high energy density, draws considerable interest. As a primary fuel for nuclear reactors, uranium supports the generation of low-carbon electricity which is vital for addressing global energy requirements and minimizing greenhouse gas emissions. The development of nuclear power indicates a rising demand for uranium resources. The stable and sufficient supply of uranium is vital for the expansion and sustainability of nuclear power. Unfortunately, the terrestrial uranium ore is limited which hampers the long-term sustainability of the nuclear industry [1]. It is critical to explore alternative methods for obtaining uranium, such as extracting uranium from seawater, wastewater or saline lakes. On the other hand, the nuclear industry produces a substantial volume of uranium-containing wastewater. Uranium, a long-lived actinide element, has radioactive, biological and chemical toxicity. It always exists as the hexavalent form in aqueous solution, which is prone to migrate and spread through water media, posing risks to ecological environment [2]. Therefore, the extraction of uranium from wastewater is of great importance.

In recent years, techniques for extracting U(VI) have emerged including membrane technology [3], reduction [5], adsorption [6], ion exchange [4] etc. Notably, adsorption is commonly utilized for its simplicity and efficiency in U(VI) removal. Numerous absorbents have been explored, such as organic framework polymers [7,8], porous silica or carbon [9,10], layered double hydroxides [11], etc. However, the drawbacks of most powder adsorbents cannot be ignored. It may need time-consuming operation after adsorption and cause secondary environmental pollution. Magnetic adsorbents can address these issues, because it is easy to realize the solid–liquid isolation under a magnetic field. In particular, nano-Fe3O4 particles have aroused considerable interest owing to the paramagnetism, low cost, non-toxic and easy preparation. However, due to the poor chemical stability of naked nano-Fe3O4 and the weak affinity for U(VI), the coating strategy may be required. It is known that the nano-Fe3O4 is usually coated by the protective and functional silica [12,13], titania [14], layered double hydroxides [15], carbon [16,17], graphene oxide [18], polymers [19,20] and so on. For example, Laurence et al. [21] synthetized Fe3O4@SiO2 bearing a Schiff base ligand for the U(VI) extraction. Amidoxime functionalized Fe3O4@TiO2 was also fabricated by Zhao et al. [22]

Compared to these coating substances, mesoporous silica stands out as an ideal candidate for its ease of modification along with high porosity. Dendritic fibrous nano-silica (DFNS) is classified as a unique mesoporous silica. It possesses the advantages of open radical pores, dendritic fibrous structure, large surface area and biocompatibility [23,24]. Notably, the unique fibrous structure and open channels increase the accessible active sites, facilitating the anchoring of target ions. Even so, to boost the affinity and selectivity towards U(VI), DFNS needs the functional modification. For instance, amine [25], carboxyl, phosphate and amidoxime [26] functionalized DFNS were fabricated. The modified DFNS showed superior adsorption capabilities and better selectivity for U(VI) than the pristine DFNS. This implies that the functional modification is important in capturing U(VI).

It is highly desirable to fabricate magnetic materials for U(VI) uptake, because the composition of actual uranium-containing aqueous solution is complex. As far as we know, studies on magnetic DFNS for U(VI) adsorption remain limited. Herein, for the first time, the combination of amidoxime groups with core–shell magnetic DFNS has been achieved. A novel amidoxime-functionalized magnetic DFNS (Fe3O4@DFNS-AO) has been designed and prepared to capture U(VI) effectively. The grafted amidoxime (AO) groups show a strong affinity towards U(VI), which significantly enhances the uptake capacity and selectivity even in the presence of varying metal ions. Moreover, the magnetic nano-Fe3O4 core facilitates the convenient recovery of powdered adsorbent from aqueous solution. The DFNS shell enhances the chemical stability of nano-Fe3O4 and also endows the adsorbent abundant mesopores and provides more accessible inner surface. To evaluate the performance of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, the experiments were carried out in varying environmental situations. For a comprehensive elucidation of adsorption behavior, adsorption kinetic and isotherm models have been researched. Finally, the mechanism for the adsorption of U(VI) on Fe3O4@DFNS-AO was proposed.

Cyclohexane sodium citrate, cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, ferric chloride hexahydrate, potassium carbonate, nitric acid, isopropyl alcohol, urea, tetraethyl orthosilicate, anhydrous toluene, sodium nitrate, sodium hydroxide, sodium acetate and anhydrous ethanol were acquired from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). 3-cyanopropyltrimethoxysilane (CETES), arsenazo Ⅲ and hydroxylamine hydrochloride (NH2OH·HCl) were purchased by Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). All chemicals were used without additional purification after receipt.
The process for preparing Fe3O4@DFNS-AO is illustrated in Fig. 1.

Fe3O4, Fe3O4@SiO2 and Fe3O4@DFNS were synthesized following our prior research [27]. Amidoxime-functionalized magnetic DFNS (Fe3O4@DFNS-AO) was prepared in the subsequent steps. Initially, 1.0 g Fe3O4@DFNS was sonicated in anhydrous toluene (90 mL) for half an hour, proceeded by the dropwise addition of 3-cyanopropyltrimethoxysilane (CETES) into the aforementioned suspension under nitrogen protection. The mixture underwent refluxing at 115°C for 20 h. Afterward, the solid was isolated under external magnetic field, rinsed alternatively with ethanol and toluene, followed by overnight vacuum drying at 70 °C. The obtained product named as Fe3O4@DFNS-CN was dispersed into 50.0 mL deionized water, proceeded by the addition of the mixed aqueous solution of NH2OH·HCl (3.0 g) and sodium carbonate (2.2 g) under nitrogen atmosphere. After heating the suspension to 75°C and stirring for 7 h, the solid was separated with magnetic assistance and alternately washed with ethanol and water. Finally, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO was acquired following overnight vacuum drying at 70°C.

Transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100F) was adopted for the analysis of the microscopic morphology of the synthesized samples. The crystalline and molecular structures of the synthesized materials were examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku SmartLab SE) and Fourier transform infrared spectra (FT-IR, Thermo Nicolet iS 10). The specific surface area and pore size distribution were determined using the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) and Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) methods based on N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms. A Micromeritics ASAP 2460 3.01 analyzer was used for the measurement of N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms at −196 ℃ after degassing the samples at 110 ℃ for 10 h. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific ESCALAB Xi + ) was employed to identify the elemental composition and chemical state. The concentration of U(VI) was analyzed using a spectrophotometer at 652 nm with 0.10 % arsenazo III present. Meanwhile, the measurement of metal ion concentrations was conducted using ICP-OES in the selectivity experiments.

The U(VI) adsorption experiments were conducted in triplicate at room temperature (25 ± 1 °C) with an initial U(VI) concentration of 50 mg/L and the solid/liquid ratio was 0.4 g/L. 0.5 mol/L HNO3 or NaOH was adopted to adjust the solution pH. The solution pH was monitored by a pH meter, keeping variations within ± 0.05. Adsorption kinetic and isotherms experiments were carried out over varying contact times (0–120 min) and U(VI) concentrations (25–200 mg/L). At regular intervals, 1.5 mL samples were withdrawn and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. The U(VI) concentration in the filtrate was analyzed using spectrophotometry. The adsorption amount of U(VI) at time t (Qt, mg/g), the equilibrium adsorption amount (Qe, mg/g) and the adsorption rate (%) were determined using Eq.1, Eq.2 and Eq.3, respectively.(1)Qt=Co-Ct×V0m(2)Qe=Co-Ce×V0m(3)Adsorptionrate(%)=100Co-CeC0where V0 (mL) represents the initial volume of the solution, C0 (mg/L) denotes the initial concentration of U(VI), Ce (mg/L) signifies the equilibrium concentration of U(VI), Ct (mg/L) is the U(VI) concentration at time t (min), and m (g) stands for the mass of adsorbent.

The microstructure of the prepared materials was characterized by TEM. As shown in Fig. 2a, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exhibits core–shell structure. The radial fibers-like structure of the shell is distinctly observed, and the gaps between the fibers form the unique open pores. This agrees well with the pristine DFNS as displayed in Fig. 2a (inset) [28]. Hence, this confirms the encapsulation of Fe3O4 by DFNS and the successful construction of magnetic DFNS composite featuring a core–shell structure.

To obtain the specific surface area and pore size distributions of the magnetic materials, the N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms of Fe3O4@SiO2, Fe3O4@DFNS and Fe3O4@DFNS-AO have been analyzed. The detailed data are displayed in Table 1. Compared with Fe3O4@SiO2, Fe3O4@DFNS and Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exhibit larger specific surface area and pore volume because of the introduce of DFNS. As depicted in Fig. 2b, the N2 adsorption/desorption isotherm exhibits H3 hysteresis loop in the sample of Fe3O4@DFNS and Fe3O4@DFNS-AO. The type IV isotherm as classified by IUPAC suggests the existence of mesopores. To further clarify the pore structure, the pore size distributions are illustrated in Fig. 2c. Fe3O4@DFNS-AO has an average pore size of around 10 nm close to that of Fe3O4@DFNS (12 nm). This suggests that the pore of Fe3O4@DFNS has no obvious blockage after modification with amidoxime group.

As displayed in Fig. 3a, the stretching and bending vibrations of −Si-O- was observed at the peak located at 1096 cm−1, 803 cm−1 and 465 cm−1 [29]. For Fe3O4, the peak at 586 cm−1 belonged to Fe-O stretching vibration[30]. Meanwhile, in the samples of Fe3O4@DFNS, Fe3O4@DFNS-CN and Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, this peak of Fe-O can also be observed, further confirming that Fe3O4 was successfully combined with DFNS. For Fe3O4@DFNS-CN and Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, owing to the modification by CETES, the appearance of C–H vibrations at 2929 cm−1, 2879 cm−1 and 1442 cm−1 suggests the presence of –CH2. Furthermore, as depicted in Fig. 3b, the spectra of Fe3O4@DFNS-CN reveals a characteristic peak for the cyano group at 2256 cm−1 [31], while it disappears after treatment by NH2OH·HCl in the spectra of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO. This indicates –CN converted to the amidoxime group completely. Moreover, the peak at 1626 cm−1 broadens, result from partial overlap of amidoxime group located at 1645 cm−1 [32].

As exhibited in Fig. 3c, in XPS spectrum of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, the intensity of C 1 s peak is enhanced and a new peak for N 1 s appears. Moreover, the high-resolution XPS spectrum is further analyzed. As illustrated in Fig. 3d, C 1 s peak of −C = N- was located at 288.78 eV. From Fig. 3e, O 1 s peak can be deconvoluted into −C = N-OH peak at 532.30 eV [33], along with Si-O peak at 532.83 eV. In addition, from the N 1 s spectrum displayed in Fig. 3f, the peak at 400.41 eV and 399.36 eV can be designated to −C = N- and –NH2 [30] resulted from the amidoxime group in Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, while there is no N 1 s peak in Fe3O4@DFNS. These results confirm the successful preparation of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO.

As displayed in Fig. 4a, the characteristic diffraction peaks at 30.1°, 35.5°, 43.1°, 57.0°, and 62.6° agree well with the (220), (311), (400), (511), and (440) crystal planes of Fe3O4 in XRD patterns(PDF#88–0866) [34]. For Fe3O4@DFNS and Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, a broad peak of DFNS appears at the 2θ position of 22.2°[29] apart from the diffraction peak of Fe3O4. This indicates the combination of Fe3O4 and DFNS, and also means the skeleton and crystal structure of Fe3O4@DFNS have not significant changes after amidoxime modification.

From the TGA curve of Fe3O4@DFNS (Fig. 4b), the total weight loss is only 6.8 % in the 30–800 °C temperature range, which may be attributed to loss of moisture as well as the residual organic matter. This indicates Fe3O4@DFNS exhibits good thermal stability. For Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, the weight loss increases as the temperature rises and reaches a plateau nearly 700 °C. Owing to the decomposition of functional groups above 100 °C, a weight loss of 5.1 % is detected. It also means the expected amidoxime functionalized Fe3O4@DFNS has been successfully synthesized.

The magnetization curve of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO is shown in Fig. 4c. The sample exhibits no remanence and coercivity, indicating the paramagnetic property. As the external magnetic field increases, the magnetization intensity gradually rises and eventually reaches saturation at 9.5 emu g−1. This suggests that Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exhibits magnetic responsiveness and magnetic-assisted solid–liquid separation can be easily achieved. Moreover, the result of water contact angle test is illustrated in Fig. 4d. The water contact angle of 36.3° indicates that Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exhibits good hydrophilicity. This promotes the wetting of the aqueous solution on the surface of absorbent, which in turn increases its interaction with uranyl ions.

The solution pH significantly impacts the distribution of U(VI) speciation and the surface charge of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, thereby altering the adsorption efficiency. Considering the hydrolysis and possible precipitation of U(VI) ions in alkaline environments, experiments on adsorption were performed in pH 3.0–7.0. From Fig. 5a, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO demonstrates the upward trend in adsorbing U(VI) with rising solution pH, while it shows weak adsorption when the solution pH ≤ 3.5. There may be two reasons for this result. On one hand, U(VI) ions predominantly exist as UO22+ (as shown in Fig. 5b). Zeta potential of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exceeds the zero point (as shown in Fig. 5c), indicating that the adsorbent exhibits a positive surface charge. Hence, electrostatic repulsion exists between the absorbent and U(VI), hindering the adsorption. Moreover, the competition of hydrogen ions with U(VI) cannot be ignored. As pH increases, the zeta potential of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO changes from positive to negative and U(VI) consists mainly of (UO2)2(OH)22+, (UO2)4(OH)7+, UO2OH+, as well as (UO2)3(OH)5+ [35] (Fig. 5b). The electrostatic attraction promotes the U(VI) adsorption. Considering the adsorption efficiency and hydrolysis of U(VI), subsequent experiments are performed at optimal pH 6.0.

From Fig. 6a, the adsorption amount of U(VI) by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO increases fast during the first 20 min. The rapid adsorption results from the strong binding ability of active sites and the high concentration of U(VI) in bulk solution. The adsorption process nearly reaches equilibrium in 40 min and Qt fluctuates slightly around 90 mg/g as time increases. This is because amidoxime groups on Fe3O4@DFNS-AO are almost occupied. Hence, the process of U(VI) uptake is found to achieve equilibrium within 40 min. These binding sites and open pores in Fe3O4@DFNS-AO results in the fast capture of U(VI).

In this section, three kinetic models are adopted for the fitting of experimental data. Pseudo-first-order model is beneficial for systems where physical adsorption is predominant. Pseudo-second-order model assumes adsorption rate depends on available binding sites of adsorbents and the amount of adsorbate, often providing a better fit for chemisorption process. Lastly, the Weber-Morris diffusion model helps identify the rate-limiting steps by considering diffusion within the pores of adsorbents. This model is particularly useful for distinguishing between external mass transfer and intraparticle diffusion. These models have been represented in Eq.4, Eq.5 and Eq.6 [36,37].(4)lnQe-Qt=lnQe-k1t(5)tQt=1k2Qe2+tQe(6)Qt=kwt1/2+Cwhere k1 (min−1), k2 (g mg−1 min−1) and kw (mg/g min−1/2) represent the rate constant of pseudo-first-order model, pseudo-second-order model and Weber-Morris diffusion model. C is the thickness of the boundary layer.

The fitting result is presented in Fig. 6 and Table 2. Pseudo-second order model fit the experimental data better than the other two models with higher value of coefficient (R2 = 0.9998). Qcal e (91.7mg/g) closely matches the experimental data (91.6mg/g). This indicates that chemisorption is the dominant mechanism in the U(VI) adsorption process. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 6d, the linear correlation coefficient of the fitting curve of Weber-Morris diffusion model is not high (R2 = 0.4556), indicating U(VI) diffusion does not mainly govern the rate.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Impact of U(VI) concentration and temperature
ce:section.ce:para: Compared with Fe3O4@SiO2 and Fe3O4@DFNS, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO can adsorb more U(VI), as depicted in Fig. 7a. This can be explained from two aspects. The incorporation of DFNS has enhanced the porosity of the absorbent, promoting the mass transfer of uranyl. In addition, the introduction of amidoxime group supplies more active sites, facilitating the U(VI) uptake. As shown in Fig. 7b. the adsorption amount of U(VI) by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO rises and then maintained steady with rising equilibrium concentrations of U(VI). The adsorption amount of U(VI) is observed to increase with rising the temperature from 25 ℃ to 45 ℃. This indicates that the adsorption is favored by elevated temperatures. It can be interpreted that at higher temperature, more uranyl ions in the liquid phase transfer to the solid surface of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO, thereby enhancing the adsorption [37].

Langmuir and Freundlich models have been adopted and these isotherm equations are as follows [38].(7)Qe=CeQmKL1+KL(8)Qe=KFCe1/nwhere KL (L/mg) is the constant of Langmuir isotherm model. KF (g−1 mg1-1/n L1/n) and n are the constants of Freundlich isotherm related to the adsorption capacity and
intensity, respectively. Qm is the maximum adsorption capacity.

The isotherm fitting result is displayed in Fig. 7c, 7d and Table 3. The experimental data is fitted better by Langmuir model, which is evident from the correlation coefficients of 0.9571, 0.9472, and 0.9529. Hence, this suggests that U(VI) can be absorbed by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO in a relatively uniform monolayer.

To measure the adsorption efficiency of materials, adsorption capacity is one of the most vital factors. The value of Qm obtained from Langmuir model is determined as 175.4 mg/g (25 ℃). This is superior to the other magnetic silica (Fig. 8). The incorporation of magnetic DFNS and amidoxime groups result in the large adsorption capacity, which enhance the mass transfer of U(VI) ions and available binding sites.

Actual nuclear wastewater typically contains a high concentration of salts. Expriments focused on the influence of ionic strength have been carried out under different NaNO3 concentration. As demonstrated in Fig. 9a, the U(VI) adsorption onto Fe3O4@DFNS-AO has a negligible dependency on ionic strength. The result implies inner-sphere surface coordination predominantly drives the U(VI) uptake, thereby substantiating the function of amidoxime groups in chelating uranyl ions.

For practical purposes, the impact of metal ions was studied with concentration of K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Cs+, Sr2+and Eu3+ equivalent to U(VI). From Fig. 9b, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO demonstrates an adsorption rate of 72.4 % for U(VI), significantly exceeding the rates for other metal ions. This indicates Fe3O4@DFNS-AO shows a remarkable selectivity for U(VI). This selectivity may arise from the strong binding ability of amidoxime groups toward uranyl because the U-nitrogen bond is shorter in length than the corresponding metal-nitrogen bonds[42].

Reusability is crucial for determining the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of absorbents. The elution in HNO3 (0.1 mol/L) facilitates the regeneration of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO-U. Given the poor stability of Fe3O4 in acidic conditions, the acid tolerance of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO was evaluated ahead of the desorption. According to Fig. 8c, the amount of leached Fe is 0.12 mg/L after 9 h of immersion. This indicates that Fe3O4@DFNS-AO has good acid resistance. In the adsorption/desorption experiments presented in Fig. 9d, the adsorption efficiency is 80.4 % during the initial adsorption and remains 68.1 % in the fifth adsorption experiment. The slight decline can be attributed to insufficient elution of uranyl ions, leaving some adsorption sites still occupied. Overall, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO exhibits good acid stability and reusability.

For the sample of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO-U, EDS spectrum displays distinct peaks corresponding to the uranium element (Fig. 10a). Based on the semi-quantitative analysis, the uranium content is about 0.58 %. This means U(VI) was captured successfully by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO. Meanwhile, from the FT-IR spectra (Fig. 10b), O = U = O stretching vibration can be observed at the wavenumber of 907 cm−1. Normally, the wavenumber is located at 925 cm−1 for uranyl nitrate [46]. The redshift of the wavenumber demonstrates that uranyl ions has interacted with Fe3O4@DFNS-AO.

In XPS survey spectra (Fig. 10c), characteristic C, N, O and Si peaks can be observed, while the iron peak cannot be observed. This further confirms that Fe3O4 is coated by DFNS, making it difficult to be detected on the surface of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO by XPS. Additionally, for Fe3O4@DFNS-AO-U (Fig. 10d), typical double peaks (382.03 eV and 392.82 eV) are assigned to U 4f [47]. This further demonstrates that Fe3O4@DFNS-AO effectively adsorbed U(VI). To elucidate the interrelationship between Fe3O4@DFNS-AO and uranyl, detailed analysis of the high-resolution spectra has been conducted. As shown in Fig. 10e, O 1 s XPS spectra can be fitted into two components. One peak at 532.83 eV corresponds to Si-O, while the other peak at 532.30 eV belongs to −C = N-OH in the amidoxime groups [33]. After U(VI) adsorption, O 1 s peak in Si-O has almost no change, while that in −C = N-OH have shifted from binding energy of 532.30 eV to 533.34 eV. Moreover, the new O 1 s peak appearing at 531.61 eV is associated with uranyl [48]. Similarly, N 1 s spectrum (Fig. 10f) includes −C = N- and –NH2 peaks at 400.41 eV and 399.36 eV [49], respectively. After the U(VI) uptake, these two peaks of N 1 s have shifted to 400.94 eV and 399.70 eV, respectively. The reason for the red shift corresponds to the reduction of electron cloud density, because oxygen and nitrogen atoms can donate lone pair electrons and coordinate with U(VI). This suggests amidoxime groups are primarily involved in the complexation and U(VI) adsorption. Therefore, surface complexation is the primary mechanism for the U(VI) adsorption by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO.

Given the analysis mentioned above, the adsorption mechanism is depicted schematically in Fig. 11. At the optimal pH 6.0, the electrostatic attraction occurs between negative Fe3O4@DFNS-AO and positive uranyl ions. This facilitates the approach of uranyl onto the absorbent. Additionally, the open fibrous architecture of Fe3O4@DFNS-AO promotes U(VI) diffusion and significantly increases the accessibility of binding sites. Because amidoxime groups have affinity toward U(VI), these U(VI) ions can be selectively absorbed onto Fe3O4@DFNS-AO by means of complexes involving amidoxime groups.

In our work, a novel magnetic amidoxime-functionalized DFNS was successful fabricated for U(VI) capture. The equilibrium of U(VI) absorbed by Fe3O4@DFNS-AO was achieved in 40 min. The adsorption capacity (175.4 mg/g, 25 ℃) was superior to other magnetic silica materials. Moreover, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO demonstrated excellent selectivity and reusability. Chemisorption was the primary mechanism governing the adsorption, with U(VI) forming a uniform monolayer on the Fe3O4@DFNS-AO surface. According to XPS analysis, amidoxime groups acted as electron donors, binding with U(VI) ions and promoting their efficient capture. Thus, Fe3O4@DFNS-AO is an attractive material for uranium separation from nuclear waste solutions.
